# No Man's Sky – 97 Hours Played and Still Exploring!

**Recommended – An Incredible Space Exploration Experience**

After spending 97 hours playing No Man's Sky, I can safely say this is one of those games where you can easily lose track of time. There's always something new to discover, another planet to explore or another objective to complete.

**Graphics and Atmosphere**

Playing at 4K on my RTX 4090, No Man's Sky can look absolutely stunning. From colourful alien planets and vast oceans to enormous space stations and impressive starships, the sheer variety of environments is one of the game's biggest strengths.

Flying through space, landing on an unexplored planet and discovering what it has to offer never really gets old. The sense of scale and freedom is fantastic.

**Exploration and Gameplay**

What makes No Man's Sky special is the freedom to play however you want. You can explore planets, discover new star systems, build bases, trade resources, upgrade your equipment, fight space pirates or simply travel around the galaxy.

There isn't just one way to enjoy the game, and that's what keeps it interesting.

The procedurally generated universe is enormous, and even after 97 hours, I feel like I've only scratched the surface of what's available.

**Progression and Upgrades**

One of the most addictive aspects is improving your equipment, expanding your inventory and upgrading your starships, multitool and exosuit.

There's a real sense of achievement when you finally obtain that upgrade you've been working towards.

The missions, guilds and reputation systems also provide plenty of reasons to keep exploring different star systems.

**Performance and Optimisation**

On a powerful PC, No Man's Sky offers a visually impressive experience, especially at 4K.

With a Ryzen 7 7800X3D, RTX 4090 and 64GB RAM, I have plenty of hardware available to enjoy the game's detailed environments and impressive space scenery.

**Things That Could Be Improved**

The inventory management can sometimes feel unnecessarily complicated, particularly when juggling resources, upgrades and storage.

Some missions can also become repetitive, and the game doesn't always explain certain mechanics particularly well. I've occasionally found myself having to work things out through trial and error.

However, these are relatively minor frustrations compared with the sheer amount of content and freedom the game provides.

**Final Verdict – 97 Hours Played**

No Man's Sky is an excellent example of a game that offers tremendous freedom, exploration and long-term enjoyment.

After 97 hours, I'm still discovering new things, upgrading my equipment and finding reasons to visit another star system.

If you enjoy open-world exploration, space travel, upgrading equipment and games that allow you to progress at your own pace, there's an enormous amount to enjoy here.

**Overall: Highly Recommended – 9/10**

*97 hours played | PC | RTX 4090 | Ryzen 7 7800X3D | 4K Gaming*

I really love games about space - mysterious, dark space, where the wonder of the unknown drives you forward to keep exploring, to be amazed by what you find, and to admire the views. Elite Dangerous once gave me those exact feelings. Despite all the empty planets and a tiny inhabited bubble, flying to the center of the galaxy and exploring was genuinely fascinating.

No Man's Sky, on the other hand, offers none of that. In fact, it actively pushes you away from exploration because there’s mountains of stuff everywhere around you. A gorgeous universe that just needs a bit more life.

The graphics are stunning. I play on ultra with a Ryzen 7 9800X3D, RTX 5090 and 32 GB of DDR5, and it runs great. My only technical complaint is the pop-in, especially when flying low in your ship. Watching rocks and plants suddenly appear really breaks the immersion.

I love the exploration, though maybe I just haven’t played enough yet. Still, planets could use more points of interest. Settlements are fine, but I miss proper cities with busier NPC activity and more established civilizations on the surface, not just space stations.

I’d also love to see more interaction between fauna and flora, something like RDR2, where you can watch predators hunt, animals feed, and creatures react to each other. Don’t get me wrong, the universe does feel alive to some extent, but it’s missing that extra layer.

Even so, I recommend it. It’s a unique, beautiful experience, and with livelier planets it could be the ultimate space game.

A very enjoyable and very well made game. 
1) Massive amounts of exploration capabilities
- Quintilions of different planets/solar systems with different animals, climates, Minerals, and plants
- Interesting side missions/quests
- Random buildings to either loot or interact with npcs
2) Fun building system
- Similar to games like ARK where you have modules that clip into each other making it simple to make structures and possible to make complex structures
3) interesting story
- cool stories both main line and side quests
4) Massive multiplayer and party system
- you can join your friends directly and you can even go out and find them without joining off them (If you can actually find them in the vast depth of space)
5) Customizable Ships/characters
- Customization is fairly interesting as for ships you can find ships you like dissassemble them for one of their core parts and make new ships with them
- Character customization is fairly vast with both accessories and the race of character

There is much much more interesting things you can do like fishing, making music, and Customizing whole space stations

2 somewhat frustrating things would be 
1) poor power scaling of you/enemies, and lack of outer space fighting diversity 
- If you get an S class ship/Multi tool you will do more damage yes but the enemies do as well also giving them more HP in some cases an upgraded ship/tool makes fights longer/harder than they would have with a c/b class ship or tool (This is easily fixed by making enemies strong based on system type/conflict levels while also making some systems actually scary to go to rather than always killing the enemies at the same pace)

THIS NEXT PIECE IS MORE FOR DEV TEAM THAN IT IS PLAYERS LOOKING TO PLAY
- This is probably one of the bigger problems of the game being that you find 1 type of outer space enemy (pirates/sentinels) and nothing more I think adding more diversity in outer space like a cosmic horror esq fight, fights from your space ship attacking a base on a planet (similar to some pirate attacks against towns), or even you could have fights where you bring your freighter to fight against say the cosmic horrors, Space stations, or even other pirate freighters

2)Occasional building/land bugs 
- when you transfer freighters base setup sometimes it will break and some of your setup will be gone/broken
-because of the land generation and because of multiplayer bugs on occasion you will get stuck underground while trying to land or your base/home may be temporarily underground (while it updates what is loaded)

I will say just this: The lack of depth stems from one's incapability to engage with their own imagination. It also comes from being unwilling to appreciate what another group of individuals have created, and this purpose becomes apparent after spending a bit of time with the game. The purpose from my viewpoint is that this game was designed as a Sandbox. What is a Sandbox? A Sandbox is something that is designed in such a way where the depth is dependent on your ability to engage. 

I used to play in an actual Sandbox when I was a child. Therefore, I am a Sandbox expert. 

The layman knows there is only sand in the Sandbox, but the expert understands that it is up to you to actually play in the sand, rather than just sit in it.

I've been playing this game since the beginning. I thought it was good back then. Just the thought of going from planet to planet across a seemingly endless galaxy was unheard of back when this game came out. It was a little bare bones back then, but it was still fun. 
I kept coming back to it on and off, and each time it got better, with more stuff to do. They just keep expanding. I don't have any other game like this that just keeps adding fun stuff to do without making me pay for another season pass or expansion pack. 
This game is a grind, but its one you want to do. I'm just going to list out some of the many things you can do in this game: Build your own starship, buy a starship, or find a crashed one. Build a bigger starship that's a mobile base and take your friends along for a ride. Fly from planet to planet, star system to star system, even discover new galaxies. Look for different minerals, scan different flora and fauna. Recruit your own animals, feed them, challenge other animals in a mini game. Like geology? enjoy finding strange rock formations. Paleontology? find bones and assemble them to make a fossil. Build a farm and grow some crops, collect milk and eggs from strange creatures, cook strange dishes. Go fishing. Build bases across the galaxy. One base for farming, one for mining, one on an asteroid, one on a nice beach planet with a chair so you can sit down and enjoy the view.  Find stuff in space, find stuff on varied planets, find stuff underground, find stuff underwater. Learn language word by word by talking to different aliens. Customize your character, your multitool, your spaceship, your bases, your space freighter, your star base. 
I'm getting tired of listing stuff, but it goes on and on. I have games that do one or two of these things, but none of them with the depth of this game. Almost ever time you play this game you will see something new. 
If you don't have this game yet, why not? This game continually grows and unlike others, so far I have never had to buy an expansion pack or season pass or in game currency. If you think it gets repetitive or too much of a grind, go play something else for a while, then come back. There will be new stuff to do, or find, or new places to explore. 
This is probably the best purchase in a long term video game I have made that I come back to again and again. I hope Hello Games continues to show every other game company how it is done.

No Man's Sky is a fun sandbox, and that's about it.

The progression loop is the best part. Building bases is genuinely fun, and maxing out your exosuit, exocraft and ship is weirdly addictive. But once you've got everything, there's nothing to use it on. No real endgame, so all that gear just sits there.

Nothing else picks up the slack. The story is okay and you can tell they tried, but it's too abstract, and digging through lore to make sense of it feels like homework. Maybe five NPCs are memorable; the rest are procedurally generated filler. Combat is bland on foot and in space, with almost no enemy variety.

Exploration is what keeps it going. There are tons of cool planets to land on, stare at, and leave. But that's the whole loop: see it, move on. Nothing makes you want to stay.

I think the problem is the procedural generation itself. A smaller, handcrafted galaxy with a tighter story and better characters would've given all those systems a reason to matter.

Worth playing if you want a chill sandbox. Just don't expect much more.
